Robert Pont
rob'ert pont
n. (Robert Pont, 1524–1606, Scottish minister, moderator and senator of the College of Justice)
Germanic Robert, bright in fame; French Pont, a bridge, from Latin pons.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Robert Pont was six times moderator of the General Assembly, minister of St Cuthbert's in Edinburgh, provost of Trinity College, and for some years a Lord of Session — a judge of Scotland's supreme civil court while serving as a minister, which the Assembly eventually decided a minister should not do and he gave up. He helped revise the Second Book of Discipline, worked on the Scottish psalm book, and wrote on chronology and on the reckoning of the year. His career raises the question of the two kingdoms in an unusually concrete form, because he held offices in both at once and the church itself made him choose. The Scottish answer was not that the civil office is unclean, nor that the minister is above it, but that the two callings are distinct and one man cannot discharge both: the church has no sword and the state has no pulpit, and a man sitting in the Court of Session cannot also sit in judgment on that court from a pulpit. “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines session as the sitting of a court or assembly for the transaction of business, and jurisdiction as the legal power of exercising authority.

expand to see more

SES'SION, n. The actual sitting of a court, council or legislative body; the time of such sitting.

JURISDIC'TION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws.

MOD'ERATOR, n. The president of an ecclesiastical assembly.

CHRONOL'OGY, n. The science of time; the method of measuring or computing time by regular divisions.

Key Scripture

Mat 22:21 — "They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's."

Rom 13:1 — "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God."

2Ti 2:4 — "No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier."

Modern Corruption

Six times moderator, and a minister made to choose between the pulpit and the bench.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs in both directions from this case. One side reads the Assembly's ruling as clericalism, the church fencing its men off from public life; the other reads it as a doctrine that civil office is beneath a Christian. Neither is the Scottish position. The civil magistracy is honourable and is itself called a ministry of God; what the Assembly denied was that one man may hold both offices at once.

The principle to recover is the distinction the Lord draws without abolishing either side of it: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21). Both have things that are theirs. Paul gives the practical reason a minister should not be entangled: “No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier” (2Ti 2:4).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek apodidomi (G591), to render, to give back what is due; empleko (G1707), to entangle, to involve.

Greek apodidomi (G591) — to give back, to render what is due; Matthew 22:21.

Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, right, power; Romans 13:1.

Usage

"“Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's” (Mat 22:21) — a Lord of Session in a pulpit."

"“No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life” (2Ti 2:4) — the Assembly's ruling."

"“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the Second Book of Discipline."
